summary: Defines how to use a JSON Web Token (JWT) as a bearer credential with OAuth 2.0, either to request an access token or to authenticate a client. It is a profile of the assertion framework in RFC 7521 and is widely used for service-to-service authentication.

plainLanguage.summary: A program shows a small signed note, called a token, to prove who it is, instead of typing a password. The server checks the signature and hands back a pass to use its services.

subtitle: How to use a signed JSON Web Token as an OAuth 2.0 login credential or as a way to get an access token.

tldr.problem: OAuth 2.0 clients sometimes already have a trust relationship with an authorization server, expressed in a signed token, and want to use it without a user-approval step. They also need a way to authenticate to the token endpoint that is not a shared password.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC profiles the assertion framework of RFC 7521 for JWTs. It defines a grant type and a client assertion type whose value is a single JWT, plus ten validation rules the authorization server must apply to that JWT.
tldr.outcome: A JWT can serve as an authorization grant, as client authentication, or both. Replay protection is optional, and the parties must agree on issuers, audiences and keys out of band.

today: RFC 7523 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2015, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains the definition of the JWT profile for OAuth 2.0 client authentication and authorization grants.

sections.title: Two Uses for a JWT in OAuth
sections.content:
A JSON Web Token (JWT) is a JSON-based security token that lets identity and security information be shared across security domains. OAuth 2.0 lets a client get an access token from an authorization server using an authorization grant, and it allows new extension grant types and new client authentication methods to be defined.

This RFC profiles the abstract assertion framework of RFC 7521 for JWTs. It defines two things: a way to use a JWT Bearer Token to request an access token when the client wants to use an existing trust relationship, without a direct user-approval step at the authorization server, and a way to use a JWT for client authentication.

The two uses are separable. Client authentication with a JWT is only an alternative way to authenticate to the token endpoint, and it must be combined with some grant type to form a complete request. A JWT grant may be used with or without client authentication; whether it is needed is a policy decision of the authorization server. How the client obtains the JWT in the first place is out of scope.

The format and processing rules are intentionally similar, though not identical, to the SAML profile in RFC 7522, which has the same authors.
sections.plainLanguage: A signed note can be used in two ways: to ask for a pass, or just to prove who you are at the door. You can do either one, or both.

sections.title: HTTP Parameter Bindings
sections.content:
For an authorization grant, the client sends an access token request as defined in RFC 7521, with grant_type set to urn:ietf:params:oauth:grant-type:jwt-bearer. The assertion parameter MUST contain a single JWT. The scope parameter may be used to indicate the requested scope. Client authentication is optional here, so client_id is only needed when the chosen form of client authentication relies on it.

For client authentication, client_assertion_type is urn:ietf:params:oauth:client-assertion-type:jwt-bearer and client_assertion holds a single JWT. It MUST NOT contain more than one JWT.

The RFC shows both forms as form-encoded POST requests to a token endpoint. In the second example the client authenticates with a JWT while presenting an authorization code grant, which shows that the two uses can be mixed with other grant types.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two labeled boxes on the form. Put the note in the first box to ask for a pass, or in the second box to prove who you are.

sections.title: What the Server Must Check in the JWT
sections.content:
The authorization server MUST validate the JWT against a list of criteria before issuing an access token or relying on the JWT for client authentication. It may add further restrictions as policy.

  • iss MUST be present and identify the issuer. Issuer values are compared with Simple String Comparison as defined in RFC 3986, unless an application profile says otherwise.
  • sub MUST be present. For a grant it typically identifies the authorized accessor, though it may be a pseudonymous or anonymous value. For client authentication it MUST be the client_id of the client.
  • aud MUST be present and identify the authorization server. The token endpoint URL MAY be used as the value, and the server MUST reject any JWT that does not name it as an audience.
  • exp MUST be present, and the server MUST reject a JWT whose expiration has passed, allowing for clock skew. It may also reject an expiration that is unreasonably far in the future.
  • nbf and iat MAY be present. A token must not be accepted before nbf, and a server may reject an iat that is unreasonably far in the past.
  • jti MAY be present. A server MAY keep the set of used jti values for as long as the JWT would be valid, to block replays.

Finally, the JWT MUST be digitally signed or have a Message Authentication Code (MAC) applied by the issuer, and the server MUST reject an invalid signature or MAC. It MUST also reject a JWT that is not valid in all other respects per the JWT specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The server is a careful doorman. It checks who made the note, who it is about, that it is addressed to this very door, that it has not run out of time, and that the signature is real.

sections.title: Error Responses
sections.content:
If a JWT used as a grant is invalid, or the current time is outside its valid window, the server returns an OAuth 2.0 error response whose error value MUST be invalid_grant. It may add detail in error_description or error_uri. The RFC's example is an HTTP 400 response with the description Audience validation failed.

If the JWT used for client authentication is invalid, the error value MUST be invalid_client.

When client credentials are present on a grant request, the server MUST validate them, even though client authentication is otherwise a policy decision.
sections.plainLanguage: If the note is no good, the doorman says no and says which kind of no it is: a bad note for a pass, or a bad note for proving who you are.

sections.title: A Worked Grant Example
sections.content:
The RFC gives a concrete example. A JWT is issued and signed by https://jwt-idp.example.com. Its subject is mailto:mike@example.com and its audience is https://jwt-rp.example.net, an identifier the authorization server uses for itself. The JWT also carries an nbf and an exp claim and one custom claim.

The JWT header declares signing with ECDSA P-256 SHA-256 using the key identified by the kid value 16. The client then sends the encoded JWT as the assertion in a POST to the token endpoint at https://authz.example.net/token.oauth2.
sections.plainLanguage: The example is a note from one company saying that Mike is a member, addressed to a particular server, with a start time and an end time, and signed with a named key.

sections.title: Agreements Needed Out of Band
sections.content:
Interoperable deployments require the parties to agree on several things, and the RFC explicitly leaves how they do so out of scope. The list is: the issuer and audience identifiers, the location of the token endpoint, the key used to apply and verify the signature or MAC, one-time use restrictions, the maximum JWT lifetime, and the specific subject and claim requirements.

Other profiles may constrain or prescribe these values. The RFC names OAuth 2.0 Dynamic Client Registration, OpenID Connect Dynamic Client Registration 1.0 and OpenID Connect Discovery 1.0 as examples. It also makes RS256 from JSON Web Algorithms a mandatory-to-implement signature algorithm for this profile.
sections.plainLanguage: Before this works, the two sides must already agree on names, keys and rules, like friends choosing a secret handshake beforehand.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 7521, RFC 6749 and the JWT specification all apply. This RFC adds one point: it does not mandate replay protection for JWT use as a grant or for client authentication. It is an optional feature that implementations may employ at their discretion.

On privacy, a JWT may contain sensitive information, so it should only be sent over encrypted channels such as TLS. If some information should be hidden from the client, the JWT should be encrypted to the authorization server. Deployments should put only the minimum necessary claims in the JWT, and sub can be an anonymous or pseudonymous value.
sections.plainLanguage: The note might have private things written on it, so send it only in a locked box, and write down only what the server needs to know.

items.label: Issuer
items.desc: Required. Unique identifier of the entity that issued the JWT.

items.label: Subject
items.desc: Required. For client authentication it must be the client_id.

items.label: Audience
items.desc: Required. Must identify the authorization server.

items.label: Expiration time
items.desc: Required. Limits the time window during which the JWT can be used.

items.label: Not before
items.desc: Optional. Time before which the token must not be accepted.

items.label: Issued at
items.desc: Optional. Time at which the JWT was issued.

items.label: JWT ID
items.desc: Optional. Unique identifier, usable for replay detection.
